title: 22. Interview: Message Queues
summary: Interview Q&A for Message Queues — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Message Queues interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Contrast a message queue with a database table used as a queue (a "todo" table polled by workers). Why is a queue better?
**Answer:** A database table can serve as a queue: producers `INSERT`, workers `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, process, and `DELETE`. This works at small scale and avoids introducing a broker. It breaks down at scale for four reasons. First, polling cost: workers must poll continuously, generating load proportional to worker count, not message rate — a 100-worker fleet polling every 100ms issues 1000 queries/sec even when idle. Second, lock contention: `SELECT FOR UPDATE` serializes on the table's lock manager, capping throughput at the database's lock throughput (typically a few thousand tx/sec). Third, visibility timeout is hard: a worker that crashes mid-process leaves the row locked or in an "in_progress" state, requiring a separate sweeper job to redeliver. Fourth, the database is not optimized for the queue workload (high write rate, low retention, hot rows) and competes with the OLTP workload for cache and I/O. A broker like RabbitMQ or SQS is purpose-built: it pushes (no polling), uses a log-structured store (no lock contention), tracks visibility natively, and isolates the queue workload from the database. The architect's rule: a DB-as-queue is acceptable below ~100 msgs/sec; above that, use a broker.
**Visual:**
```
DB queue:        INSERT -> poll (1000 q/s) -> SELECT FOR UPDATE -> DELETE
                 lock contention caps at ~5k tx/s, sweeper for crashes
broker queue:    enqueue -> push to consumer -> ack -> log-structured store
                millions/sec, no polling, native visibility, isolated from DB
```

### Q2. What is the visibility timeout, and what happens if you set it too low or too high?
**Answer:** The visibility timeout is the window during which a delivered message is invisible to other consumers — the broker assumes the original consumer is still processing. If the consumer acks within the window, the message is removed; if not, the message becomes visible again and is redelivered to another consumer. Set it too low (e.g., 5 seconds for a 30-second processing job) and the broker redelivers while the original consumer is still healthy, causing duplicate processing — at-least-once delivery becomes effectively many-times-once. Set it too high (e.g., 12 hours for a 1-second job) and a crashed consumer blocks redelivery for hours, leaving messages stranded and inflating end-to-end latency. The right value is `processing_p99 × 2`, with a floor of 30 seconds and a ceiling of a few minutes for most workloads. AWS SQS allows up to 12 hours, useful for long-running batch jobs where the consumer is single-threaded and crash recovery is rare. RabbitMQ uses a similar concept called `consumer timeout` (default 30 minutes). Kafka does not have visibility timeouts because it is pull-based: a consumer holds its offset and advances it after processing; a crash triggers a rebalance and the new consumer resumes from the last committed offset, redelivering uncommitted messages.
**Visual:**
```
visibility=5s, processing=30s  -> msg redelivered 6x while healthy (duplicates)
visibility=12h, processing=1s  -> crash blocks redelivery for 12h (stranded)
visibility=2*p99 (e.g. 60s)    -> crash redelivers in ~1 min, no false dupes
```

### Q3. Why does AWS SQS standard queue not guarantee FIFO, and when must you use SQS FIFO?
**Answer:** SQS standard queues are designed for nearly unlimited throughput (no per-queue cap) and at-least-once delivery, which they achieve by sharding internally and allowing parallel consumers to receive messages out of order. The trade-off is that strict ordering is impossible when multiple consumers pull in parallel — the broker cannot know which consumer will ack first. SQS FIFO queues enforce strict ordering by serializing all message groups through a single shard, capping throughput at 300 msgs/sec (3000 with batching) per queue. Use FIFO when ordering matters: financial transactions (a debit must precede a credit), stateful workflows (create_user before charge_user), or any pipeline where reordering causes incorrect results. Use standard when ordering does not matter and throughput does: log ingestion, telemetry, independent notifications. The architect's rule is to default to standard and switch to FIFO only when a documented correctness requirement demands it, because FIFO's throughput limit is real and will bite you at scale. Netflix's billing pipeline used FIFO for charge events (ordering critical) and standard for analytics events (ordering irrelevant), running both through the same SQS account.
**Visual:**
```
standard:   P --msgs--> [shard1, shard2, ...] -> parallel consumers (unordered, ~unlimited tput)
FIFO:       P --msgs--> [single shard]        -> one consumer at a time (ordered, 300/s)
use FIFO:   financial txn, stateful workflow (create -> charge -> ship)
use std:    logs, telemetry, independent notifications
```

### Q4. How does a priority queue work, and what are its operational pitfalls?
**Answer:** A priority queue maintains messages in priority order, so a higher-priority message always dequeues before a lower-priority one regardless of arrival time. RabbitMQ implements this with a heap per queue, supporting up to 255 priority levels; the producer sets `priority=N` on publish. The operational pitfalls are starvation, head-of-line blocking, and noisy-neighbor effects. Starvation: if high-priority traffic is sustained, low-priority messages never dequeue — Instagram's verified-account notifications could starve normal-account notifications during a celebrity event. The fix is aging: gradually increase a waiting message's priority over time so even low-priority messages eventually dequeue. Head-of-line blocking: a single high-priority message that crashes its consumer blocks the entire queue's high-priority lane until retries exhaust — combine with a short visibility timeout and a DLQ to clear it fast. Noisy-neighbor: a single tenant flooding high-priority traffic starves all other tenants; the fix is per-tenant priority queues with a fair scheduler across tenants. The architect's rule is to use priorities sparingly — most workloads are fine with a single queue and FIFO. Reserve priorities for genuine urgency (incident alerts, payment failures) where delaying a low-priority message is preferable to delaying a high-priority one.
**Visual:**
```
queue with priorities 0-9:
  P=9 [alert: payment failed]  -> dequeues first
  P=5 [notification: like]     -> dequeues when no P>=6 messages
  P=1 [analytics: page view]   -> starves if P>=2 traffic sustained

pitfalls: starvation (use aging), HoL blocking (DLQ fast), noisy neighbor (per-tenant Q)
```

### Q5. What is delayed delivery, and how do you implement a 24-hour delay in a queue that only supports 15 minutes?
**Answer:** Delayed delivery enqueues a message that becomes visible to consumers only after a specified delay — useful for reminders ("send a follow-up email in 24 hours"), retry backoff ("retry this failed job in 1 hour with exponential backoff"), and scheduled workflows. SQS supports up to 15 minutes via `DelaySeconds`; RabbitMQ supports arbitrary delays via the `rabbitmq_delayed_message_exchange` plugin (storing messages in a Mnesia table keyed by due time); Kafka does not support per-message delays natively. For a 24-hour delay when the broker caps at 15 minutes, the standard pattern is a delay chain: enqueue to `delay-15m` topic; a poller consumer picks it up after 15 minutes and re-enqueues with `delay_remaining - 15m` to another `delay-15m` topic; after 96 hops (24h / 15min), the message lands in the final delivery topic. A simpler alternative is a separate scheduler: a cron job (or a Quartz scheduler, or a DynamoDB table with TTL) stores `(due_time, msg)` and a sweeper runs every minute, dequeuing due messages and enqueuing them to the real queue. Netflix's reminder service uses a DynamoDB table with TTL + a Lambda sweeper, supporting arbitrary delays with no broker changes. The trade-off is operational complexity: the delay chain is self-contained but introduces 96 hops of failure surface; the external scheduler is simpler but adds a component to operate.
**Visual:**
```
SQS DelaySeconds: max 900s (15 min)
24h delay options:
  chain:    Q15m -> poller -> Q15m (96 hops) -> Qfinal   (self-contained, fragile)
  scheduler: store (due, msg) in DynamoDB+TTL -> Lambda sweep every 1 min -> Qfinal
                                                (simpler, extra component)
```

### Q6. Compare RabbitMQ, SQS, and Kafka as message queue technologies.
**Answer:** RabbitMQ is a traditional AMQP broker optimized for low-latency, feature-rich queuing: priorities, routing (topic exchanges), transactions, and per-message ack. It scales to ~50k msgs/sec per node and is run as a cluster of Erlang nodes; its strength is flexibility, its weakness is throughput. SQS is a fully-managed AWS service optimized for hands-off operation: no clusters to run, automatic sharding, multi-AZ durability, and infinite throughput on standard queues. Its strength is zero-ops, its weakness is feature poverty (no priorities, limited routing, 15-min max delay) and vendor lock-in. Kafka is a distributed log optimized for high-throughput streaming: millions of msgs/sec per cluster, partitioned topics, consumer groups, and long retention (days to weeks). Its strength is throughput and replayability, its weakness is that it is a log, not a queue — no priorities, no per-message delays, and individual-message ack is replaced by offset commits. The architect's decision tree: use RabbitMQ when you need priorities, routing, or per-message transactions under 50k/sec; use SQS when you want zero-ops and are already on AWS; use Kafka when you need streaming throughput, replay, or multi-consumer fan-out. Many production systems use two: Kafka for the high-volume event stream and RabbitMQ or SQS for the low-volume control plane.
**Visual:**
```
RabbitMQ: ~50k/s, priorities, routing, transactions, self-hosted Erlang cluster
SQS:      ~unlimited/s (std), 3k/s (FIFO), zero-ops, AWS-only, few features
Kafka:    millions/s, partitions, consumer groups, replay, log (not queue)
pick:     RabbitMQ=features<50k; SQS=zero-ops AWS; Kafka=streaming/replay
```

### Q7. What is the difference between persistent and non-persistent delivery, and when does non-persistent make sense?
**Answer:** Persistent delivery writes each message to disk (and replicates it) before acking the producer, so the message survives a broker crash. Non-persistent delivery keeps messages in RAM only, acking as soon as the message is in memory — much faster (10x–100x) but the message is lost if the broker crashes. RabbitMQ marks messages with `delivery_mode=2` (persistent) or `1` (non-persistent); ActiveMQ uses a similar flag. Non-persistent makes sense when the message is reproducible (a cached state update that can be re-derived), when the cost of persistence dominates (very high rate, small payload), and when the broker's uptime is high enough that the expected loss is acceptable. The canonical use case is a real-time analytics stream where the source system can replay the last hour from its own logs if the broker crashes — losing 5 minutes of in-flight data is fine because it can be regenerated. The architect's rule is to default to persistent for any message that represents a user action or financial event, and to consider non-persistent only for telemetry, caching, and ephemeral state. ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ both crashed in production at scale when operators defaulted to non-persistent and then lost data on a broker restart — a mistake that has cost real money.
**Visual:**
```
persistent:     enqueue -> write disk -> replicate -> ack   (crash-safe, ~10k/s)
non-persistent: enqueue -> store RAM -> ack                  (crash loses, ~100k/s+)
use non-persistent: reproducible telemetry, cache updates, ephemeral state
use persistent:     user actions, financial events, anything not replayable
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Netflix's "video viewed" pipeline enqueues events to SQS, consumers load to Redshift. A consumer fails after dequeue but before the Redshift load, and the visibility timeout expires. Describe what happens and how to prevent data loss.
**Answer:** When the visibility timeout expires, SQS assumes the consumer died and makes the message visible to other consumers, redelivering it. With at-least-once delivery, another consumer picks up the message and loads it to Redshift — but if the original consumer was just slow (not dead), it may finish the load after the redelivery, causing a duplicate row in Redshift. The fix has two parts. First, make the Redshift load idempotent: use the event's `event_id` as the primary key and `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING` (or use a staging table with `MERGE`), so duplicate loads are no-ops. Second, tune the visibility timeout to `processing_p99 × 2` (e.g., if the Redshift COPY takes 60 seconds p99, set visibility to 120 seconds), so a healthy but slow consumer does not trigger redelivery. Third, monitor `ApproximateReceiveCount` per message — if it exceeds 1, alert, because it means visibility timeouts are firing on healthy consumers and the timeout needs to increase. Netflix's actual pipeline does exactly this: the COPY is idempotent via `event_id` dedup, visibility is 5 minutes, and the dashboard tracks receive count as a health metric. The result is no data loss (messages always redeliver) and no duplicates (idempotent load), at the cost of occasional re-processing that the database absorbs.
**Visual:**
```
consumer dequeues msg, visibility=30s, Redshift COPY takes 60s
  -> 30s expires -> SQS redelivers to consumer 2
  -> consumer 2 COPYs the same row -> duplicate (without dedup)
FIX:
  1. INSERT ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING -> idempotent
  2. visibility = 2 * p99(COPY) = 120s -> no false redelivery
  3. monitor ApproximateReceiveCount > 1 -> alert, raise visibility
```

### Q2. Instagram's notification pipeline uses RabbitMQ priority queues: priority 9 for verified accounts, priority 1 for normal. During a celebrity event, normal users see 5-minute delays. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** The diagnosis is priority starvation: sustained priority-9 traffic from the celebrity event monopolizes consumers, and priority-1 messages accumulate without dequeueing. The fixes, in order of escalation. First, add priority aging: every minute a message waits, its effective priority increases by 1, capped at 8 — so a priority-1 message that has waited 8 minutes reaches priority 9 and dequeues. This bounds the maximum delay for any message to roughly `(max_priority - initial_priority) minutes`, here 8 minutes. Second, add a separate queue for verified-account traffic: route priority-9 messages to a dedicated queue with a small consumer fleet, and priority-1 messages to the main queue with a large fleet. This isolates the noisy neighbor (the celebrity) from normal users — verified users get their 1-second SLA, normal users get their 30-second SLA, and neither starves the other. Third, autoscale the main queue's consumer fleet on queue depth: when depth exceeds 1000, HPA adds pods. The architect's rule: priorities are a sharp tool that causes starvation; prefer per-class queues with separate fleets whenever you can afford the operational cost. Instagram moved to per-class queues in 2017 after a Kim Kardashian post caused exactly this starvation; the engineering blog post-mortem is required reading.
**Visual:**
```
before: 1 queue, P9 (verified) starves P1 (normal) -> 5 min delays
fix 1:  aging: P1 msg waits 8 min -> P9 -> dequeues (max delay 8 min)
fix 2:  2 queues: Q_verified (small fleet, P9), Q_normal (large fleet, autoscale)
fix 3:  HPA on Q_normal depth>1000 -> add pods
result: verified 1s SLA, normal 30s SLA, no starvation
```

### Q3. Uber's trip-completion events must be processed in order per trip, but the broker is SQS standard (no FIFO). How do you enforce ordering?
**Answer:** SQS standard does not guarantee FIFO across consumers, so application-level ordering is required. The pattern is to use a per-trip sequence number and a reorder buffer. The producer (the trip-completion service) attaches `trip_id` and `seq` to each event (e.g., `trip_id=T1, seq=1` for "trip started", `seq=2` for "trip ended"). The consumer maintains an in-memory buffer keyed by `trip_id`, storing out-of-order events. When it receives `seq=2` for `T1` but has not seen `seq=1`, it buffers `seq=2` and waits. When `seq=1` arrives, it processes `seq=1`, then `seq=2`, then advances the per-trip cursor. If `seq=1` never arrives (lost or delayed), a timeout flushes the buffer with a warning, accepting the gap. The alternative is to migrate to SQS FIFO with `MessageGroupId=trip_id`, which gives strict per-trip ordering at the cost of 300 msgs/sec per queue (3000 with batching) — for Uber's 200k events/sec, this would require ~70 FIFO queues sharded by `trip_id` hash, which is operationally complex. The architect's decision: at low rate (per-trip events, not per-event), FIFO is fine; at high rate, application-level ordering with a buffer is the right trade-off. Uber eventually migrated to Kafka with `trip_id` as the partition key, getting both ordering and throughput — SQS was a stopgap.
**Visual:**
```
SQS standard (no FIFO):
  producer: trip_id=T1, seq=1  ->  SQS  ->  consumer A (processes seq=1)
            trip_id=T1, seq=2  ->  SQS  ->  consumer B (buffers, waits for seq=1)
            trip_id=T1, seq=3  ->  SQS  ->  consumer C (buffers)
  reorder buffer per trip_id; advance cursor on contiguous seq
alternative: SQS FIFO + MessageGroupId=trip_id -> 3000/s, need ~70 queues
best:        Kafka, key=trip_id -> per-trip partition, ordering + throughput
```

### Q4. You deploy RabbitMQ with persistent messages and confirm mode (publisher confirms). Throughput drops from 50k/s to 5k/s. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** The diagnosis is that persistent messages plus publisher confirms force an `fsync` per message: the broker writes the message to disk, calls `fsync` to flush it to the physical medium, and only then sends the confirm to the producer. With one `fsync` per message and a disk that fsyncs at ~1ms, throughput is capped at ~1000 msgs/sec per queue. The fixes, in order of throughput recovery. First, batch confirms: the producer sends a batch of messages and waits for a single confirm for the batch, reducing per-message round trips — RabbitMQ's `async` confirms handle this. Second, batch fsync: RabbitMQ can be configured to fsync every N messages or every T milliseconds (via the `disk_monitor` and the `msg_store` settings), trading a small window of crash-induced data loss for 10x throughput. Third, use a faster disk: NVMe SSDs fsync at ~50µs instead of ~1ms, recovering most of the throughput. Fourth, partition the workload across multiple queues: RabbitMQ's per-queue throughput is limited by the Erlang process for that queue, so 10 queues sustain 10x the throughput of one. Fifth, consider moving to Kafka: Kafka batches writes by design (500ms or 1MB, whichever comes first) and sustains millions of msgs/sec because it does one fsync per batch, not per message. The architect's rule: persistence is expensive, batch it, and pick the broker whose batching model fits your throughput target.
**Visual:**
```
persistent + sync confirm: 1 msg = 1 fsync (1ms) = 1000/s per queue
fix 1: async confirms (batch ack)              -> ~3k/s
fix 2: batch fsync (every N or T ms)           -> ~10k/s (small crash-loss window)
fix 3: NVMe disk (fsync 50µs)                  -> ~20k/s
fix 4: 10 queues (parallel Erlang processes)   -> ~100k/s
fix 5: Kafka (batch fsync by design)           -> millions/s
```

### Q5. YouTube's video-upload pipeline enqueues transcoding jobs to SQS. A 4K video takes 30 minutes to transcode, but SQS visibility timeout maxes at 12 hours. Some jobs are redelivered mid-transcode, causing duplicate work. How do you fix it?
**Answer:** The visibility timeout should be set to `processing_p99 × 2`, but for a 30-minute job, that means a 60-minute visibility timeout — well within SQS's 12-hour max. The duplicate work means the timeout is set too low (perhaps the default 30 seconds), causing SQS to redeliver while the transcoder is still working. The fix is straightforward: set `VisibilityTimeout=3600` (1 hour) at enqueue time or per-dequeue via `ChangeMessageVisibility` to extend it as the job progresses. The deeper fix is to use a heart-beat pattern: the consumer periodically calls `ChangeMessageVisibility` to extend the timeout by another interval (e.g., every 5 minutes, extend by 10 minutes), so the visibility timeout tracks the actual processing progress and never expires while the consumer is alive. If the consumer crashes, the heart-beat stops, the visibility expires, and SQS redelivers. This is the standard pattern for long-running jobs: YouTube's transcoders extend visibility every minute, AWS's own batch-processing services (Lambda, ECS) do the same, and the SQS docs explicitly recommend it for jobs longer than the visibility max. The architect's rule: for any job longer than 5 minutes, use a heart-beat; for jobs longer than 12 hours, switch to a workflow engine (Step Functions, Airflow) that does not rely on a single visibility timeout.
**Visual:**
```
30-min transcode, visibility=30s (default) -> 60 redeliveries, 60x duplicate work
FIX:
  set VisibilityTimeout=3600 (1h) at enqueue, OR
  heart-beat: consumer calls ChangeMessageVisibility(+600) every 5 min
    -> visibility tracks actual progress, never expires while alive
    -> crash stops heart-beat -> visibility expires -> redeliver (correct)
long jobs (>12h): use Step Functions (no single visibility timeout)
```

### Q6. Amazon's order-placement pipeline uses SQS FIFO with `MessageGroupId=order_id` for per-order ordering. A single high-volume order (10k events in 1 minute) blocks the queue. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** SQS FIFO serializes all messages with the same `MessageGroupId` through a single shard, so a single `order_id` with 10k events serializes through one shard, capping that order's throughput at 3000 msgs/sec (the FIFO cap) and blocking other orders that hash to the same shard. The diagnosis is hot MessageGroupId: a single group monopolizes a shard. The fixes, in order. First, change the MessageGroupId to a finer-grained key: if the order has 10k events, partition them by `order_id + event_type` or `order_id + seq/100`, so events for one order spread across multiple shards. The trade-off is that ordering within the order is now per-sub-group, not per-order — acceptable if sub-groups are independent (e.g., payment events and shipping events can be processed in parallel). Second, split the order's events across multiple FIFO queues, sharded by sub-group hash, so each queue's 3000/sec cap multiplies. Third, reconsider whether FIFO is needed at all: if the events are independent (e.g., telemetry about the order, not state transitions), use SQS standard and accept unordered delivery. Amazon's actual pattern uses a mix: state transitions (create, pay, ship) go through a FIFO queue keyed by `order_id` for strict ordering; telemetry goes through a standard queue for throughput. The architect's rule: FIFO's 3000/sec cap is per MessageGroup, not per queue — design the group key to spread load, or pay the throughput price.
**Visual:**
```
1 order, 10k events, MessageGroupId=order_id -> serialized through 1 shard
  -> 3000/s cap, blocks other orders on same shard

fix 1: MessageGroupId=order_id+event_type (payment | shipping | telemetry)
  -> spreads across shards, ~3x throughput, per-sub-group ordering
fix 2: multiple FIFO queues, shard by sub-group hash -> 3k * N queues
fix 3: state transitions on FIFO (order_id), telemetry on standard (no order)
```

### Q7. You migrate from RabbitMQ to Kafka for higher throughput. The team complains that they lost the priority queue feature and the per-message delay feature. How do you implement these in Kafka?
**Answer:** Kafka does not natively support priorities or per-message delays because it is a log, not a queue. The workarounds are idiomatic but require redesign. For priorities, use multiple topics: `events.high`, `events.normal`, `events.low`. The consumer subscribes to all three and Kafka delivers in topic-order, so the consumer drains `events.high` before `events.normal` before `events.low` — but Kafka does not strictly interleave, so the consumer must poll all topics and pick the highest-priority available message programmatically. A simpler approximation is to consume only from `events.high` if it has messages, otherwise from `events.normal`, otherwise from `events.low` — implemented with separate consumers or with a polling strategy that checks lag. For per-message delays, use a tiered delay topic pattern: the producer writes to `delay-5s` with a `due_at` header; a poller reads from `delay-5s` after 5 seconds and either delivers to the final topic or re-enqueues to `delay-1m` for a longer delay; chain these for arbitrary delays. Alternatively, use an external scheduler (DynamoDB with TTL + Lambda sweeper, or Quartz) for delays longer than a few minutes. The trade-off is operational: RabbitMQ gives you these features for free at low throughput; Kafka requires you to build them but gives you millions of msgs/sec. The architect's rule: if priorities and delays are central to your business (e.g., a hospital alerting system), stay on RabbitMQ; if throughput is central, move to Kafka and pay the feature-reimplementation cost.
**Visual:**
```
priorities in Kafka:
  topics: events.high, events.normal, events.low
  consumer: poll all, prefer high (or consume high first, then normal, then low)

delays in Kafka:
  tiered: produce to delay-5s -> poller after 5s -> deliver OR re-enqueue to delay-1m
  external: DynamoDB TTL + Lambda sweep (for > 5 min delays)

trade-off: Kafka = build features, get millions/sec
           RabbitMQ = free features, ~50k/sec
```
